clue.text: Both Mr Universe and Miss World must have this VIP!

definitions.text: Both Mr Universe and Miss World must have this
definitions.meaning: contest winners for physique and beauty must possess a fine figure, read here as two words meaning a certain physique
a very important person, someone of consequence

explanation.surface: A quip about what beauty-pageant and bodybuilding champions share, ending on their celebrity status.
explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer into two words and it becomes what every pageant winner needs: 'some body'.
explanation.definitionFit: A person of importance is colloquially called a big name or a someone, a synonym for a VIP.

clue.text: See 26
True to Englishwoman, new groom may fear this plant!

definitions.text: True to Englishwoman, new groom may fear this plant!

parts.words: True to Englishwoman, new groom may fear this plant
parts.note: the plant is a succulent named after that sharp speech

explanation.surface: A newly married Englishman fears a certain houseplant, in the spirit of mother-in-law jokes.
explanation.definitionFit: Sansevieria, a succulent with long sharp-edged leaves, is popularly named after a wife's mother's cutting speech.

clue.text: See 12
I send SOS in trouble and strife

indicators.note: trouble means disturb or stir up, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone in trouble sends a distress call, with 'trouble and strife' also being rhyming slang for wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trouble and strife' reads as a stock phrase (Cockney rhyming slang for wife), but 'trouble' is the anagram signal and 'strife' the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Disagreement and conflict within a group is strife, so the two words are synonyms.

clue.text: See 21
Percival wants something to knock down Round Table colleague

parts.note: Lance Percival was a British comic actor and singer
an auctioneer knocks down a lot to the highest bidder

explanation.surface: Sir Percival needs a jousting weapon to unhorse a fellow knight of the Round Table.
explanation.walkthrough: Percival looks like the Arthurian knight, but here he is Lance Percival, a 1960s British entertainment figure. 'knock down' is auction language, not jousting.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Lancelot was one of King Arthur's knights, so a fellow member alongside Percival at the Round Table.

clue.text: Growths of wage structure within Liverpool FC?

indicators.note: within places the rearranged letters inside the football nickname

parts.note: Liverpool Football Club are nicknamed the Reds

indicators.note: a wage structure suggests the letters of wage are rebuilt into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A question about the growth of the pay structure at Liverpool football club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wage structure' reads as a stock phrase about pay, but 'structure' is the anagram signal and 'within' the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Ragwort and similar weeds are growths, plants that spring up uninvited, so the plural fits as an example.

clue.text: So straight trainee beats trainer to work?

parts.note: L stands for learner, as on a learner driver's plate
someone who arrives before the boss is in early

explanation.surface: An eager apprentice arrives before the coach, a picture of a keen start to the day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trainer' suggests a running shoe or a coach; the phrase simply means arriving early. L for learner is a standard UK learner-driver sign.
explanation.definitionFit: Moving in a straight line means proceeding directly, so the adverb describes going straight.

clue.text: Coming after the event at half ten's not so restricting

indicators.note: restricting means hemming in, so the phrase for 'not so' holds the other pieces
half here trims the three-letter number word down to its last two letters

explanation.surface: Someone arriving at half past ten finds the rules relaxed, as if punctuality were negotiable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half ten' looks like a clock time (British for 10:30), but 'half' cuts the word TEN to EN.
explanation.definitionFit: Arriving after the event is the very state of tardiness, the noun naming a late coming.

clue.text: See 26
'Princess' taking Ecstasy yet? Laid-back youngster's initially denied being one?

definitions.text: 'Princess' taking Ecstasy yet? Laid-back youngster's initially denied being one?

indicators.note: laid back read as lying backwards, so the assembled pieces are read in reverse order

parts.note: Regan is one of King Lear's daughters, a princess
E is the usual abbreviation for the drug ecstasy

indicators.note: denied means refused, so a letter is withheld from the word yet
initially points to the opening letter of youngster's

explanation.surface: A worried parent asks whether a spoiled 'princess' is on drugs yet, picturing a laid-back adolescent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially denied' takes the Y of 'youngster's' from YET, leaving ET; 'Laid-back' reverses REGAN + E + ET. The whole clue also describes the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue paints a pampered, drug-curious, laid-back adolescent, exactly the stereotype of a person in their teens.

clue.text: See her on a merchantable cast?

definitions.text: See her on a merchantable cast?

indicators.note: cast means thrown into a new shape, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A suggestion to watch an actress among a commercially bankable film cast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cast' looks like a film's line-up, which suits this actress, but it is the anagram signal for 'her on a merchantable'.
explanation.definitionFit: The British actress is a box-office name, the kind you see in a saleable film ensemble.

clue.text: Rears of loose horses impede getting across awesome fence — earnest prayers needed!

indicators.note: getting across means spanning, so the fence word straddles the end letters

parts.note: Becher's Brook is a fearsome fence in the Grand National steeplechase

indicators.note: rears means the back ends, the final letter of each of the three words

explanation.surface: A racing scene: loose horses in the Grand National hamper others at a fearsome fence, and punters pray.
explanation.walkthrough: BECHERS is Becher's Brook, a notorious fence in the Grand National, Britain's famous steeplechase. 'Rears of' gives ESE, which BECHERS gets across.
explanation.definitionFit: Those who beg and implore are people praying earnestly, with 'prayers' meaning people who pray.

clue.text: A "bargain" has nothing in free of foreign bodies

indicators.note: has means holds, so the bargain word contains what follows
in places the zero inside the word for free

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: An advert boasts a bargain that is entirely free of foreign bodies, as if contaminant-free goods came cheap.
explanation.walkthrough: 'free of foreign bodies' reads as one phrase, but 'free' gives RID and 'of foreign bodies' is the definition. 'in' puts O in RID; 'has' puts ROID in STEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: Asteroids are rocky bodies from space, so the adjective describes things relating to such alien objects.

clue.text: Occupier of soup kitchen beds up with cricketer and a good book

indicators.note: in a down entry, up means the word reads from bottom to top

parts.note: KP is Kevin Pietersen, the England batsman
OT is the Old Testament, part of the Good Book

explanation.surface: A charity scene: someone at a soup kitchen beds down beside a cricketer with a Bible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupier of soup kitchen' suggests a homeless person, but it is the pot of stock sitting in the kitchen.
explanation.definitionFit: A large pot for simmering stock is a fixture of any soup kitchen's stove.

clue.text: Fantastic repartee where game bird takes seasonal occupation

definitions.text: where game bird takes seasonal occupation

indicators.note: fantastic means fanciful or wild, so the letters are recombined

explanation.surface: Witty banter about where a game bird sets up for the season.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition alludes to the carol 'The Twelve Days of Christmas', whose partridge sits in this tree.
explanation.definitionFit: The carol's partridge sits in one at Christmas, so it is the bird's festive perch.

clue.text: One regularly in possession of secret tapes got mugged

definitions.text: One regularly in possession of secret

indicators.note: mugged means roughed up, so the letters are knocked into a new order

explanation.surface: A spy thriller: someone holding secret tapes gets mugged.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on the idiom 'between you, me and the post', said when sharing a confidence.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom names this post as a party to secrets, so it is often in on confidences.

clue.text: Worms backward class will cage to make more docile

indicators.note: backward tells us to read the whole assembly from right to left
will cage means will enclose, so the class word holds the rest

parts.note: a set is a class or group in a school

explanation.surface: A teacher plans to calm a backward class by caging them, a grimly comic classroom scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'backward class' suggests a slow group, but 'backward' reverses the whole of SET caging DO + TAMER, giving SEDOTAMERT read backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: Flukes are parasitic flatworms, and this is the zoological name for that class of worms.

clue.text: See 2
See 2
Eves?

parts.note: Eve was the ... human created after Adam, so several Eves would be more than one such figure

explanation.surface: A one-word puzzle about the biblical first woman.
explanation.definitionFit: Grammar's 'you' plural is the second person plural, and Eve was the Bible's second person, so many Eves fit.

clue.text: See 12
Strangely unrecognised, dine out on this?

definitions.text: Strangely unrecognised, dine out on this?

indicators.note: strangely signals the letters of unrecognised are rearranged, with the letters of dine taken out

explanation.surface: An unknown diner eats out on something they haven't paid for, unnoticed.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove D, I, N, E from UNRECOGNISED ('dine out') and rearrange the rest. The whole clue also hints how a freeloader eats.
explanation.definitionFit: To cadge or beg food and favours from others is how a freeloader manages to eat out without paying.

clue.text: See 21
The old girl snuggles in under bootless military leader

indicators.note: snuggles in means nestles inside, so the old girl sits within the other word
bootless means without its foot, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: an old girl, informally, is a grandmother, a gran

explanation.surface: An elderly woman snuggles up beneath a barefoot general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bootless' looks like a description of the leader, but it removes the foot (final letter) of the word for 'under'.
explanation.definitionFit: Manuel Belgrano was an Argentine general of the independence wars; a warship sunk in the Falklands bore his name.

clue.text: Ungulates dispersing after second ceremonial blast

indicators.note: after places the scrambled animals behind the number

parts.note: second is the first word of 21-down's answer, so it stands for 21

indicators.note: dispersing means scattering, so the letters of the animals are rearranged

explanation.surface: Hoofed animals scatter after a second blast of a ceremonial salute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second' looks like a time unit, but it refers to 21-down, whose answer begins with that word: so it means twenty-one.
explanation.definitionFit: Firing twenty-one guns is the traditional honour salute for heads of state at ceremonies.

clue.text: Given value from shepherdesses, say, looking the other way?

indicators.note: looking the other way means facing backwards, so the extracted letters are read right to left
from signals the letters are taken out of the run of words that follows

explanation.surface: Shepherdesses appear to be valuing something while averting their eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' picks DESSESSA out of 'shepherdesses, say', and 'looking the other way' turns it round.
explanation.definitionFit: To appraise something is to give it a value, as an assessor or valuer does.
